stances.claim: People's Initiative (PI) cannot be used for federalism because the Supreme Court held in Lambino v Comelec (Oct 25, 2006) that only minor amendments -- not complicated matters altering the government's nature and structure -- can be the subject of this mode, leaving Con-ass and Con-con as the only viable methods.

Under Con-ass, the chambers should vote separately -- 'If ordinary legislation is separately voted upon, why should the remaking of the most fundamental law be treated any less stringently?' -- using the a-fortiori logic that the more fundamental act deserves at least the procedural protections of the less fundamental.
stances.rhetorical_move: a-fortiori argument (more fundamental act needs at least equal procedural protection)

stances.claim: Con-con is the preferred method -- the President favors it per media reports, it avoids the joint-or-separate dilemma, and unlike Congress it can devote full time to exhaustively discuss federalism and other proposed constitutional changes (like parliamentary system); given Duterte's huge popular mandate, the 2/3 vote needed should not be difficult.

The timeline is tight: Alvarez's June 30 Con-con bill awaits July 25 session, three readings in both chambers + public hearings + plenary debates on many delegate-design questions (election method, party-list inclusion, incumbent-kin restrictions, nonpartisan rules), then Comelec needs at least 6 months to prepare -- making 2018 the earliest convening, plus Con-cons historically take at least a year, plus a 60-90-day plebiscite window after approval; the ultimate question is whether the new Constitution takes effect during or after Duterte's term.

While the Con-con process unfolds, Congress should rush ordinary legislation for other urgent reforms -- tax restructuring, emergency powers for Metro Manila traffic, comprehensive peace agreements with Muslim brethren and the NDF, wider agrarian reform, and Local Autonomy Code amendment to devolve more powers to LGUs -- making parallel-track reform the prudent strategy rather than waiting for federalism.
stances.rhetorical_move: parallel-track recommendation (don't wait for Cha-cha; rush ordinary legislation)

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban continues his federalism series (after Federalism 101 on June 5 and Federalism 102 on June 12) by discussing how the system can be instituted. Charter change ('Cha-cha') would undoubtedly be needed; the 1987 Constitution provides three methods -- people's initiative (PI), constituent assembly (Con-ass), and constitutional convention (Con-con) -- all requiring electoral ratification via plebiscite. PI cannot be used because Lambino v Comelec (Oct 25, 2006) limits it to minor amendments, not complicated nature/structure changes like federalism. Under Con-ass, Congress (3/4 vote) directly proposes the changes; the big issue is joint vs separate chamber voting, and CJ argues for separate voting via a-fortiori logic: 'If ordinary legislation is separately voted upon, why should the remaking of the most fundamental law be treated any less stringently?' Fortunately, the President per media reports favors Con-con, avoiding the joint-or-separate dilemma and allowing dedicated full-time deliberation of federalism plus other proposed changes (like parliamentary system). Under Con-con mode, Congress convenes the convention by 2/3 vote (or submits to electorate by majority); Duterte's huge mandate makes 2/3 attainable even with separate chamber voting (2/3 = 16 of 24 senators for Con-con call; 3/4 = 18 for Con-ass approval). Incoming Speaker Pantaleon Alvarez took the first step by filing a Con-con bill on June 30, but it can only be taken up when Congress opens session July 25 -- undergoing three readings in both chambers, public hearings, plenary debates on many design questions (all elected or ex-officio, how many, by what method, party-list inclusion, incumbent-kin eligibility, partisan rules); lawmakers will protect their political turf. After bill passage, Comelec needs at least 6 months to prepare (manual or automated), suggesting the Con-con election coincide with October 2016 barangay elections (possibly postponed) or May 2019 congressional elections to save costs (P6.26B was 2016 election cost) and minimize election fatigue for Comelec, public school teachers (Board of Election Inspectors), watchdogs, and voters. The earliest convening is 2018; Con-cons historically take at least a year; a 60-90-day plebiscite window follows approval. The ultimate question: will the new Constitution take effect during or after Duterte's term? Meanwhile, Congress should rush ordinary legislation for non-federalism reforms the President and Cabinet are raring to implement -- tax restructuring, emergency powers for Metro Manila traffic, comprehensive peace agreements with Muslim brethren and the National Democratic Front, wider agrarian reform, and amendment of the Local Autonomy Code to devolve more powers to LGUs.
